title: Characterization tests
summary: Untested legacy code gets pinned by tests that describe what it currently does, not what it should, so a safe refactor has something to check against.
signals: a hot, frequently-changed file with no tests at all
"don't touch this, nobody knows why it works" comments
magic numbers and deeply nested conditionals with no names for the rules they encode
a bug report about behaviour that turns out to be undocumented, not obviously wrong

roles.computeRefund(): the legacy operation under study: no tests, several undocumented rules
roles.legacy.computeRefund: the original implementation, left untouched, that the characterization tests pin
roles.refactored.computeRefund: the same behaviour with named helpers and constants, proven identical by the same test table
roles.the characterization test table: the sensing variable: one row per input the team has now bothered to observe and pin
roles.the odd behaviours: the 14/15-day boundary and the >30-day rounding - undocumented, not yet judged as bugs

stages.title: Before
stages.idea: The legacy computeRefund has nested conditionals, magic numbers, and no tests. One test only pins that it exists and runs for a single sample input - the starting point of legacy work, not a spec.

stages.title: After
stages.idea: A table of characterization tests pins the CURRENT output for every case that matters, including the odd ones, each named "currently ..." instead of "should ...". A refactored implementation with named helpers and constants passes the exact same table, proving the redesign changed nothing observable.

checks: Why is the before-stage test named "nobody knows what computeRefund does" instead of describing a requirement?
Why are the after-stage test names "currently ..." instead of "should ...", and what would change if they said "should"?
The 14-day/15-day boundary and the >30-day rounding look like bugs. What has to happen before either one gets "fixed", and how would that step differ from writing a characterization test?
If someone changed the refactored implementation to give a full refund on day 15 instead of 90%, which specific test fails, and why does the legacy assertion in that same test keep passing?
